hd.hero.k: Fifty years of computing, under one finger
hd.hint.gate: Press and hold, or scroll.Anywhere, or the space bar.
hd.hint.gate.t: Press and hold, or scroll.Here, or on the square.
hd.hint.run: Keep holding, scroll, or drag the curve.Every beat doubles them.
hd.hint.look: Keep holding, and look around.Move over the square: it is not the same everywhere.
hd.hint.look.t: Keep holding, and look around.Slide over the square: it is not the same everywhere.
hd.hint.coast: The easy years.Let go for a moment: it rolls on by itself.
hd.hint.pay: Heavier now.Every generation costs more than the last.
hd.hint.moment: Try it.Hold or scroll on whenever you like.
hd.m.one: A transistor: a switch with no moving parts. Current wants to cross from the source to the drain, and the gate decides. No current is 0; current is 1. Everything a computer does, it does with these.
hd.m.on: 1. Charge on the gate opens a channel under it, and current crosses. Let go and it falls back to 0: that is one bit. Now keep holding.
hd.m.double: Every beat, twice as many, in the same space.
hd.m.garage: 1,200 transistors: a chip one person made in a garage, in 2021.
hd.m.rule: Twice as many about every two years, because the lines a chip is drawn with kept getting finer: the line width beside the count, in micrometres (µm, thousandths of a millimetre), later in nanometres (nm, millionths). For fifty years that was the whole plan.
hd.m.coast: The easy years. A smaller transistor was also a faster and a cheaper one, so it nearly ran by itself.
hd.m.invisible: You can no longer see them. The glass shows what is there.
hd.m.pay: Now every generation has to be paid for. To design one leading chip:
hd.m.gaa: To keep its grip on a channel this small the gate now wraps all the way round it.
hd.m.old: With several passes of the old light, every step takes more effort.
hd.m.push: 336 billion transistors in one graphics processor of 2026, on two dies in one package. One more doubling: hold.
hd.m.wall.p: The newest generation of factory fits about 1.15 times as many transistors in the same space, not twice, and designing one chip for it costs about {design}.
hd.mo.job.q: 2,300 transistors now fit on one chip. Build a chip for one job, or one that runs any program? Slide between them.
hd.mo.job.aria: From one job to any program
hd.mo.job.0.d: A chip made for the job: nothing does it on less energy. The next job needs a whole new chip.
hd.mo.job.1.d: A processor with instructions added for this job: most of the saving, and it still runs other programs.
hd.mo.job.2.d: the energy for the same work (measured for video). In return everyone can share it, and it runs whatever comes next.
hd.mo.job.after: The world went mostly with the processor, and has argued about where this line belongs ever since.
hd.mo.job.lab: Play it: the right chip for the job
hd.mo.bug.q: A processor has shipped with five entries missing from a table inside its divider. It passed its tests. Test it yourself.
hd.mo.bug.lead: Random tests are how most checking is done.
hd.mo.bug.ran: in {n} random divisions. About one in nine billion goes wrong: at this rate, about {left} more tries to see the first.
hd.mo.bug.after: A test only shows what was tried. Its maker replaced the chips, and took a charge of $475 million.
hd.mo.bug.lab: Play it: find the copy that is wrong
hd.mo.light.q: The lines are now far finer than the light that prints them, which is 193 nm. How do you print them? Look in the glass.
hd.mo.light.one.d: Lines finer than the light blur together: look at the glass.
hd.mo.light.passes.d: Each layer printed in several passes, each lined up with the last to a few nanometres. Every step now takes more effort: you will feel it in the hold.
hd.mo.light.euv.d: A new light close to X-rays. The newest machines for it cost about {euv} each.
hd.mo.light.after: The industry did both, one after the other.
hd.mo.light.lab: Play it: print the finest lines
hd.q.label: The question behind it
hd.ways.k: What people are trying against it
hd.wall.switch.phys: Physics: kT/q × ln 10, about 60 mV for each tenfold at room temperature
hd.w.switch.q: Lower the point where the transistor turns on, so it still switches at a lower voltage. How low do you dare?
hd.w.switch.out: {n} times the leak through every transistor that is at 0, for a turn-on point {mv} mV lower. Look in the glass.
hd.w.switch.out0: Drag it down. Watch the glass, and the square behind it.
hd.w.memory.q: Where do you keep the numbers?
hd.w.memory.oa: 640 pJ (picojoules: a tiny measure of energy) to fetch 16 bits, against 0.18 pJ to add them. The trip is nearly all of the cost.
hd.w.memory.ob: 8–11 pJ to fetch 16 bits from memory on the same chip. Far better, and still many times the sum itself.
hd.w.memory.oc: ? Do the sum where the numbers are stored, and the trip is gone. What it costs instead is one of the lab’s puzzles.
hd.w.power.q: Each answer goes on getting cheaper. Where will the total be in 2030? Drag to your guess.
hd.w.power.out: {dc2030} TWh is the projection for 2030, about twice today. You said {n}: {verdict}. Cheaper answers, and the world asks for far more of them.
hd.w.power.lab: Jevons’ bet: does a better chip save energy?
hd.w.cost.q: You have {design}. How do you spend it?
hd.w.cost.oa: 1 try The squares are the price of one design, generation by generation, drawn to scale.
hd.w.cost.ob: About 100,000 tries Each dot is one run of 1,000 finished chips on an open process (worked out from the two prices). Not the same chips: far simpler ones. But a hundred thousand chances to learn something.
hd.s.c2: one dot · one run of 1,000 chips
hd.bet.switches.d: Transistors that tunnel, sheets one atom thick, carbon nanotubes: ways to turn on more sharply than this, or to stay sharp when tiny.
hd.bet.spikes.d: Neurons that fire only when something changes, each keeping what it knows beside it: one research system joins 1,152 chips into 1.15 billion neurons.
hd.arch.d: A computer is transistors arranged into gates, gates into blocks, blocks into a machine. The walls are problems of that arrangement, so people are trying other ones.
hd.arch.q1: Rise from the transistor you started with. Drag, or tap the square.
hd.lv.3.d: A transistor The one you pressed at the start: 0 or 1. Even at 0 it leaks a little: the first wall starts here.
hd.lv.2.d: A gate Four transistors wired to answer one small question about two inputs: is either of them 0? Watch them take turns.
hd.lv.1.d: A block Gates wired together to add, compare or remember. Every wire between them costs energy and time.
hd.arr.classic.d: Logic in one place, memory in another, and every number makes the trip between them. The second wall is this drawing.
hd.arr.legend: Fine grid: memory. Coarse blocks: logic. Red: a number on its way.
hd.trip.0: none, it stays where it is used
hd.arch.ch.q: Find the arrangements where a number never travels at all.
hd.arch.ch.why: In each, what a part knows is kept where it works. That saves the trip, and makes what it knows hard to copy out.
hd.mach.n: Or no fixed arrangement at all
hd.mach.d: Holding gave everyone the same computer, a little better every two years. The lab’s bet for what comes next: no standard computer at all, but a machine put together for one need, from blocks everyone shares.
hd.form.circuit.d: cheapest to run, fixed for good
hd.mach.bad: It does not meet the need: the {part} can no longer change.
hd.tri.gen.p: An agent tries every plan and offers the one no other beats.
hd.tri.gen.done: It tried {n} plans, {ok} of them meet the need, and it offers this one. It decides nothing.
hd.tri.chk.p: The numbers are computed, never claimed.
hd.tri.dec.p: Only you know what the need is really for.
hd.isle.d: A machine that is only chosen has not been designed, made, tested, shipped or used. The lab is an island built round that one loop. The lit places are what you already did on this page.
hd.tr.lab: Your machine arrives here, as something open.
hd.tr.lab.0: Nothing kept yet: your machine would arrive here, as something open.
hd.tr.studio: One job, or any program: you tried the line between them.
hd.tr.studio.go: The right chip for the job
hd.tr.fab: The light: you tried the ways to print finer than it. And the price of a try.
hd.tr.fab.0: The light, and the price of a try.
hd.tr.test: Five missing entries: you tested a chip that passed its tests.
hd.tr.test.0: Five missing entries in a table.
hd.tr.test.go: Find the copy that is wrong
hd.tr.port: Not yet. Where a chip will live decides what it must survive.
hd.tr.port.go: Send one to a phone, a car or a data centre
hd.tr.datacentre: The leak, the distance and the power: where the walls bite.
hd.tr.datacentre.0: The leak, the distance and the power bite here. You have not tried them yet.
hd.tr.datacentre.go: Dive from a data centre to an atom
hd.m.not: 2 transistors, one above the other: the simplest gate. Put 1 in and 0 comes out; put 0 in and 1 comes out. It is called NOT.
hd.mo.gate.q: Wired together, four transistors make a gate: two inputs on the left, one output on the right. Make the output 0.
hd.mo.gate.lead: Tap the inputs to switch them between 0 and 1, and watch which transistors let current through.
hd.mo.gate.yes: Only 1 and 1 make 0. This gate is called NAND (“not and”). Wire enough of them together and you can build every other circuit: an adder, a memory, a whole computer.
hd.mo.gate.lab: Play it: the gates inside a chip
hd.next.d: Fifty years of shrinking put about 146 million times more transistors on a chip. The room left now is not in size but in energy. Moving one bit from memory on another chip costs about 40 picojoules; the least physics allows for a bit is about 3 zeptojoules, some 14 billion times less.
hd.next.q: Hold, and go down, toward the floor.
hd.nx.zone: no one has a number here yet
hd.rung.far.d: Where an AI chip spends most of its energy today: every number fetched from memory on another chip, 640 pJ for 16 bits.
hd.rung.near.d: Memory on the same chip: about 8–11 pJ for 16 bits, some 70 times less. Memory stacked right beside the chip in one package, made in volume since 2026, sits between the two.
hd.rung.inside.d: Do the sum inside the memory and the trip is gone. What is left is the sum itself, 0.18 pJ for 16 bits: 3,500 times less than where you began.
hd.rung.new.d: Below the sum no one has a number yet. Switches that turn on more sharply, chips that compute only when something changes, light in place of wires: each is trying to go further down.
hd.rung.floor.d: Erasing one bit costs at least kT ln 2, about 3 zeptojoules at room temperature, and it has been measured. Computing that never erases a bit, reversible logic, could go below even this.
hd.cq.fit: In 1965 Gordon Moore guessed the count would double every year. The red line is that pace. Drag it until it runs through the chips.
hd.cq.fit.aria: How many years for each doubling
hd.cq.fit.over: At this pace a chip of 2026 would hold {x} times too many.
hd.cq.fit.under: At this pace a chip of 2026 would hold {x} times too few.
hd.cq.fit.yes: The pace Moore settled on in 1975, and chips kept to it for forty years: a rule people planned by, not a law of nature.
hd.cq.knee: Faster transistors also gave a faster clock, the beat a chip works to. Add the clock: in which year did it stop climbing? Tap that year.
hd.cq.knee.no: Not there. Look for where the red rings stop rising while the transistors go on.
hd.cq.knee.yes: At about 3.8 GHz the chip got too hot to cool. The extra transistors went into more cores instead, each running one or more threads: add the threads to see them rise.
hd.cq.guess: Last one: how many transistors will one processor hold in 2026? Guess before you get there.
hd.cq.guess.seen: You have already seen 2026. Next time, guess before you get there.
hd.cq.guess.tap: Now tap the chart at your number
hd.cq.guess.yours: Your guess: {n}. Now go on to 2026.
hd.cq.guess.out: You guessed {n}; one graphics processor of 2026 holds 336 billion, on two dies. {verdict}
hd.cq.guess.v1: Within a factor of two: you think in doublings.
hd.cq.guess.v2: Off by {x} times: close, for something that doubles.
hd.cq.guess.v3: {x} times too low. Almost everyone guesses low: doubling outruns what we can picture.
hd.cq.guess.v4: {x} times too high. Even the largest chip there is, a whole wafer made into one, holds about 4 trillion.
hd.cq.done: Twice every two years; the clock stopped, the cores took over, and the count still doubled. What comes after it?
hd.arch.q3: The fifty years were not one way of building a computer. Pick an era.
hd.era.clock.d: For thirty years the extra transistors made one core quicker: a shorter beat, and more done at each. Programs got faster without being rewritten. It ended around 2004, when the chip got too hot to cool.
hd.era.cores.d: With the clock stuck, the transistors became copies of the core, working side by side. Now a program has to be split into parts to go faster, and every core waits on the same memory.
hd.era.special.t: A chip for one kind of work
hd.era.special.d: A graphics chip does thousands of small sums at once. In 2012 a network trained on two of them beat every other way of recognising pictures, and chips made for the sums of AI followed.
hd.era.chiplets.d: One huge chip is too hard to make without a flaw, so the design is cut into small chips, made apart and joined in one package around a hub. Each part can even come from a different factory.

hd.d.lede: Fifty years of holding ended at a wall. What comes after is laid out as one chip, and the square you held is one block of it. Keep holding, or scroll: the camera goes from block to block. Or tap any block. Four of them fail a check. The pads on the edge lead out, to the island.
hd.m.named: Since about 1997 a line width is only the name of a generation of factory: nothing on the chip measures it any more, so it is in quotes.
